bib.title: Natural Language Processing with Python, Chapter 7: Extracting Information from Text
bib.venue: O'Reilly Media (book chapter; year inferred from the O'Reilly NLTK book, not printed in the chapter text)

question: How can structured data (entities and the relations between them) be extracted from unstructured text with chunking, named entity recognition and relation extraction?
contributions: Defines an information extraction pipeline: sentence segmentation, tokenization, POS tagging, entity recognition, relation recognition
Builds noun phrase chunkers with regular expressions (chunk, chink), n-gram taggers and a feature-based classifier, scoring each on CoNLL-2000
Introduces IOB tags, cascaded chunkers for nested structure, gazetteer lookup, and relation extraction by regular expressions over the string between two entities

results.claim: A chunker that finds no chunks still scores 43.4% IOB accuracy on NP chunking, because most tokens are outside any NP; precision, recall and F are all 0.
results.setup: CoNLL-2000 test.txt, chunk_types=['NP'], RegexpParser('') as baseline

results.claim: A naive regexp chunker NP: {<[CDJNP].*>+} reaches F 69.2% on NP chunking.
results.setup: CoNLL-2000 test.txt NP chunks; one-line regular expression over POS tags

results.claim: A unigram tagger over POS tags (a data-driven chunker) reaches F 83.2%.
results.setup: CoNLL-2000 train.txt to test.txt, NP chunks, UnigramChunker (POS tag to IOB tag)

results.claim: A bigram tagger chunker reaches F 84.5%, a small gain over unigram from adding the previous POS tag.
A classifier-based chunker with only the current POS tag matches the unigram chunker (F 83.2%).
results.setup: ConsecutiveNPChunker, MaxentClassifier trained with algorithm='megam', feature = pos only

results.claim: Adding the current word as a feature improves chunking by about 1.5 percentage points, about a 10% reduction in error rate.
results.setup: ConsecutiveNPChunker features pos, word, prevpos; IOB 93.6% to 94.2%, F 84.4% to 85.9%
results.quote: about 1.5 percentage points (which corresponds to about a 10% reduction in the error rate)

results.claim: Adding lookahead, paired and tags-since-determiner features lifts the chunker to F 89.5%.
results.setup: Features pos, word, prevpos, nextpos, prevpos+pos, pos+nextpos, tags-since-dt; same split

results.claim: The CoNLL-2000 corpus holds 270k words of Wall Street Journal text with three chunk types (NP, VP, PP).
results.setup: CoNLL-2000 Chunking Corpus as shipped with NLTK

limits: Every chunking score is a single train/test run on CoNLL-2000 with no variance, seeds or significance test; precision and recall use exact chunk match.
Entity recognition is shown only by gazetteer lookup and a pre-trained chunker (ne_chunk) with no accuracy number; relation extraction has no evaluation at all, only printed examples.
The classifier chunker (MaxentClassifier, megam) is a greedy left-to-right maximum entropy model with no sequence-level decoding, so it cannot revise earlier IOB tags.
The code is Python 2 and NLTK 2 (print statements, megam, nltk.sem.extract_rels signatures).
practices: Establish a trivial baseline (no chunks, then a one-line regexp grammar) before training a chunker, so a score has something to be compared with (7.2).
Use IOB tags to turn chunking into token-level tagging so ordinary taggers and classifiers apply, and convert predictions back to trees (7.3).
Build the feature set by adding one feature at a time (POS, previous POS, word, lookahead, paired, tags-since-DT) and re-score each step on the held-out set (7.3).
Do not rely on gazetteer lookup alone: location names collide with common words and with other entity types (May, North), so combine a gazetteer with context (7.5).
For relation extraction, take triples (X, string between, Y) over typed entity pairs, filter with a regular expression and expect false positives such as filler strings (7.6).

terms.definition: segmenting and labelling multi-token sequences; the pieces do not overlap in the source text
B marks the start of a chunk, I a token inside a chunk, O a token outside any chunk
removing a sequence of tokens from a chunk, the inverse of chunking
a geographical dictionary used for entity lookup
identifying mentions of potentially interesting entities and their type (ORG, LOC, PERSON, DATE...)
finding relations between pairs of named entities, here via a regular expression over the intervening words
